div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: This First Reader continues the interesting exercises of the Aldine Primer—the rhymes and stories, the dramatizations and pictures—which make the child’s efforts to master the art of reading both delightful and surprisingly successful. The content is concrete, alive and full of action. The joys of happy childhood at play in the open—with the birds, the animals, the flowers, the wind, the snow and the rain—the joys of childhood’s imagination, are presented in the language of childhood and from the child’s point of view. The child finds here none of the drudgery—to him quite meaningless—so often associated with the disagreeable task of learning how to read; the child reads from the very first page—he has been reading all through the Primer—reads with delight and real understanding, reads the thoughts and feels the pleasures of childhood. Hence the not uncommon occurrence of a child’s suddenly discovering in surprise that he has learned how to read—that he can read—that he is reading—and that he likes to read!

But there is no magic about the Aldine method, if it can be called a method. Like the marvellous modern achievements of applied science, its success depends upon the simple principle of understanding and utilizing, instead of ignoring and antagonizing, nature. The child’s nature furnishes the key, the sure guide to all the method there is in Aldine reading.

The initial stock of about one hundred “sight words,” which the reading of the Primer has furnished, is increased gradually. At first most of the new words are easily acquired, as were those of the Primer, through the memorizing of simple and interesting rhymes. Such rhymes occur on pages 3, 6, 11, 15, 17, 25, 28, 33, 37, 47, 55, 75. But for the development of the power and the habit of independent mastery of new words by the child reliance is placed on the exercises in phonics, which should be systematic and constant throughout the book. Just what these exercises are and just how they are to be carried out to make them most effective are matters fully explained in the Teacher’s Manual, “Learning to Read.”

No formidable mechanism is involved in the teaching of phonics. The plan is an entirely simple and natural one. The pupil is shown how and encouraged from the outset to do quickly, directly and intelligently what he otherwise learns slowly, indirectly and unconsciously. He is taught to observe, to analyze and to compare words; he is taught to apply constantly his growing knowledge of sounds and of letters used to represent sounds. These exercises are scarcely less interesting to the child than are the rhymes, stories and dramatizing, for the child understands what he is doing and why he is doing it, and he feels the joy of increasing mastery. So rapid and sure is the child’s progress and growth in independent power that he reads at sight and reads well any interesting Primer long before he has completed this First Reader. When this book is completed he can read any properly graded First Reader, in fact almost anything that he can understand, and he can read it absolutely at sight with little hesitation and read it with intelligent expression.

Aldine Reading, as presented in this and in the other books of the Aldine Series, is vastly more important than any mere method or device for acquiring mastery of the mechanics of reading—it does lead to that mastery speedily; it is all-round, rich, sound education for the primary child; and withal it is a joy to child and teacher, as all primary education ought to be.

div.head: With·The·Birds
div.p: Fly, little birds, to the tall tree.
Fly to your nest and little birds three.
Fly to the tall tree, little birds.
Fly to your three little birds.
Your little birds fly to the tall tree.
Your little birds fly to the nest.
Little birds, fly to your nest.

lg.l: Fly to your three little birds.
Fly to your nest and three little birds.
To the place you love best,

div.p: Fly to the place you love best.
Fly to your dear little nest.
You love the tall tree, little birds.
You love your dear little nest.
You love your three little birds best.
Your little birds fly to the tall tree.
Your little birds fly to the nest.
Your little birds love the tall tree.
Your little birds love the nest.
Your dear little birds love you best.
They are flying to the tall tree.
They are flying to the place they love.
They are flying to the dear little nest.
They are flying to three little birds.
They are flying to the birds in the nest.
They love the tree and the nest.
They love the little birds best.
Fly to the place you love best.
Fly to your dear little nest.
Your nest is in the tall tree.
Your little birds are in the nest.
Fly to your dear little birds.
Your little birds love the tree.
Your little birds love the nest.
They love the nest in the tall tree.
You love your little birds best.
Come, Robin, come and get your breakfast.
I see you, Robin, in the tree.
You are flying to the tall bough.
You are singing to your little birds.
They are in the nest in the tall tree.
The nest is on the bough.
You love your nest in the tall tree.
Fly to your dear little nest.
Robin Redbreast is singing on the bough.
It is in the tall tree.
Robin’s nest is on the bough.
He is singing to the little birds.
The little birds are in the nest.
He wants breakfast for the little birds.
Come, Robin Redbreast, come to me.

lg.l: Now you can feed your little birds.
I want to feed the little birds, too.
There is a nest in the old oak tree,
There are three tiny eggs blue as blue can be,

div.p: A nest is in the old oak tree.

lg.l: The nest is safe on a high bough.
Three tiny eggs are in the nest.
The eggs are as blue as blue can be.
There are three baby birds in the tiny nest,
And the wind rocks the bough where they safely rest,

div.p: Robin made a nest in the oak tree.
There it is high up on the bough.
Three tiny eggs are in the nest.
They are as blue as blue can be.
They are as blue as the sky.
Soon there will be three baby birds in the tiny nest.
The wind will rock the bough.
But the birds will be safe in the nest.
And they will like the wind to rock the bough.
They will sing to the little birds.

div.head: THE OLD OAK TREE
div.p: There is the old oak tree.
See the birds flying to the nest.
The nest is in the tree.
Little blue flowers grow under it.
The tree loves birds and flowers.
And they love the old oak tree.
The old oak rocks the birds in the nest.
The nest is on a high bough.
But the little birds rest there safely.
The old birds fly in to the nest.
Then they fly to the tree-top.
The little birds can not fly; they can not sing.
So they say, “Peep! peep! We love! we love!”
The little flowers look up to the old tree.
They can not fly; they can not sing.
But they, too, love the old oak tree.

lg.l: Whichever way the wind doth blow
Some heart is glad to have it so.
Then blow it east or blow it west,
The wind that blows—that wind is best.

div.head: THE WIND
div.p: The tall trees rock in the wind.
See the boughs sway up and down.
Some little birds are in their nest.
The nest is on a high bough.
They are glad to have the wind blow.
They like the west wind best.
It rocks them in their nest.
They like to rock in the tree-top.
Sing to the dear little birds.
Sing a song to the birds in the nest.
When the wind blows, the cradle will rock.
When the bough breaks, the cradle will fall,
And down will come rock-a-bye, birdies and all.”
The nest is the little birds’ cradle.
It is on a bough in the tree-top.
It rocks when the wind blows.
When the bough breaks it falls.
It falls down, down, away down!
And down fall birdies and all.

div.head: THE LEAVES
div.p: “Come, little leaves,” said the wind one day,
“Come over the meadows with me and play.”
Come and play with me, little leaves.
“Come, little leaves,” said the wind, “come with me.
Come over the meadows with me.
Come play with me in the meadows.”
One day the wind said, “Come, come with me, little leaves.
I want to play with you.

div.head: THE BIRDS AND THE LEAVES
div.p: An old oak tree grew in the meadow.
Two birds made a nest in it.
Soon there were three little birds there.
They could not fly; they could not sing.
But the old birds loved the little ones.
The little leaves looked into the nest.
They wanted to go with the leaves.
They wanted to fly from their nest.
Up blew the wind one day.
The leaves flew away with the wind.
They played in the meadow all day.
The old oak tree said, “Come to me, little leaves.”
“Come! come! come!” said the little birds.
But the leaves could not come.
They were asleep in the meadow.

div.head: THE SNOW
div.p: All summer the little birds played in the old oak tree.
They flew from bough to bough.
They rocked on the high boughs.
They played with the little leaves.
They flew up, up to the blue sky.
They flew down to see the flowers.
They flew down under the tree.
Up to the tree-top they flew again.
Whichever way they flew, they were glad.
One day the wind said, “Come, little birds.
Fly away from your nest in the tree.
The little leaves are all asleep.
The little flowers are all asleep.
The snow will soon be coming down.
How the little birds wanted to stay!
But no, they must fly away.
The wind said they must fly away.
They flew away over the meadows.
In her nest at peep of day?

lg.l: Till the little wings are stronger.”
So she rests a little longer,

div.head: LITTLE BIRDIE
div.p: Little birdie is in her nest.
“I want to fly from the nest.
Let me fly high over the tree-top.”
But the mother says, “No, no, you can not fly.
Rest in the nest a little longer.
Soon your wings will be stronger.
You can fly over the tree-tops.
You can fly over the meadows.”
So birdie will stay in the nest a little longer.
And when her wings are stronger, she will fly away.

div.head: FEEDING THE SQUIRRELS
div.p: The ground was covered with snow.
They were running over the ground.
“What can the little squirrels want?” said Baby.
The squirrels ran to the oak tree.
There are three squirrels in the tree.
We will feed the little squirrels.
There were the squirrels in the tree.
They were glad to see the acorns.
Then they ran to the old oak tree.

div.head: THE SQUIRRELS
div.p: Two squirrels made their nest in the old oak tree.
All summer they played in the shade.
They ran up and down the boughs.
In the fall the leaves flew away.
All the little birds flew away, too.
They were going away for the winter.
They were flying away from the snow.
At last the squirrels are alone.
Must they leave the old tree, too?
No, little care they for the snow.
They have a nest; they have acorns.
They will be glad all winter.
Then birds and leaves will come back.

div.head: SUMMER IS COMING
div.p: Summer is coming! Summer is coming!
How do you think I know?

lg.l: So I know it must be so.
Summer is coming! Summer is coming!
For I found a sweet blue violet,
And that is how I tell.

div.head: PUSSY WILLOWS
div.p: How do you think I know?
To-day I found some pussy willows.
Pussy willows come to tell us winter is over.
So I know that summer is coming.
And I love the dear little pussy willows.

div.head: THE PUSSIES
div.p: It was a glad spring morning.
Some little pussies were out playing.
They were playing beside the old willow tree.
Two little birds were in the tree.
They were singing a glad song.
Be glad! Be glad! Be glad!”
It was a sweet, sweet song.
It made the boys and girls glad.
But do you think it made the pussies glad?
Little cared they for the sweet song!
They said, “Now we have found some breakfast.
We will get the little birds.”
Up into the tree they jumped.
They ran from bough to bough.
“We can have no breakfast here,” said the pussies.
“We must look for some other birds.
We will jump to the ground.”
They were growing fast to the tree!

div.head: LITTLE VIOLET
div.p: She had been asleep all winter.
All winter she had been sleeping under the snow.
Blue-bird was flying from tree to tree.
He flew to the tree over Little Violet.
He was singing, “Dear Little Violet, come out, come out!
Are you not tired of winter?
Summer is coming! Summer is coming!
I am tired of winter! Tired of winter!
I love the summer! I love the summer!
Come, Little Violet, come up! I will sing to you.”
Little Violet was tired of winter.
She was tired of the snow.
She longed for the sweet singing of the birds.

lg.l: She was so glad when Blue-bird called.
She awoke. She came out. She grew.
Blue-bird and Violet were so glad.
Winter was past; summer was here.
Dear little baby, close your eye,
All little babies should be asleep,
For the stars are shining through,
And into the nest of all they peep,

div.head: MOTHER’S SONG
div.p: They are shining through the night.
They are shining into Robin’s nest.
Now the stars peep in at Baby.
Baby is going to sleep, too.
She has been playing all day.
I think you will like it, too.
Mother will sing of little sheep.
The little sheep run round and round.
The little sheep jump over the ground.
Mother is singing of little sheep.”

div.head: BABY
div.p: Baby has been playing in the meadow.
She has been playing there all day.
She has been playing hide and seek.
All day Blue-bird has been singing.
She has been singing in the meadow.
Playing and singing, singing and playing!
What a good time Baby and Blue-bird have had!
They have been glad all the day long.
Blue-bird was singing to her little ones.
Baby said she was singing to her, too.
Three little birds were in the nest.
She gave them some bread for breakfast.
“Peep! peep! Thank you! thank you!” said the little birds.
They were glad, but they longed to fly.
They wanted to fly over the tree-tops.
They were growing in the meadow.
She found a sweet blue violet, too.
Pussy willows and violet were growing there side by side.
They peeped at Baby as she came up.
Baby gave the violet to her mother.
Violet tells me summer is coming,
Summer, and the summer sky, so blue.”

div.head: BABY ASLEEP
div.p: She has played all the day long.
Mother will rock her; Mother will sing her to sleep.
Close your sweet blue eyes, Baby dear.
Little blue-birds are asleep in their nest.
Pussy willow and Violet are sleeping, too.
Close your sweet blue eyes, baby dear.
High up in the sky, they are shining through the night.
They are peeping into Blue-bird’s nest.
They see the little birds sleeping there.
They peep in at mother, rocking and singing to baby.

lg.l: They want to see baby sleeping, too.
Baby’s sweet blue eyes are closed at last.

div.head: THE NEW KITE
div.p: Who do you think made it?
Tom made the kite all alone.
“I will take my kite to the meadow,” said Tom.
Tom went out with his new kite.
But the kite did not fly well.
“I do not want to play with my kite.
It does not fly well,” he said.
I think the string should be longer.
I will get a longer string.
Some day the wind will be stronger.
I will come again to the meadow.
I will bring Baby with me.
I will fly my kite for her.”
It was a good long string.
In the morning he will go again to the meadow.

div.head: TOM AND THE WIND
div.p: He likes to play with her.
Tom likes to play with the wind, too.
And the wind seems glad to play with Tom and Baby.
To-day they were in the meadow.
The wind blew Tom’s hat away.
How it flew over the meadow!
The wind made the leaves fly round and round.
They found no place to hide.
They found no place to rest.
High, high up over the tree-tops it flew!
Then down, down, down it came.
Up, up, up, again it went.
Tom said, “It is flying to the sky.
It will fly right out of sight.”
As he said this, he let go the string.
And away went the wind with it.
Then Tom and Baby went home.

div.head: THE SONG OF THE WIND
div.p: I rock the birdies in their nest.
I sing a sweet song to them.
Winter is coming; snow is coming.
Some days I sing a loud song.
“O I am the wind and I come very fast;
Through the tall trees I blow a loud blast.”

lg.l: The beautiful summer is here again.
We have done with the winter, the snow and rain;
The flowers grow bright by the garden wall,
And the rose is the fairest one of all.
The apple tree blossoms are fair and sweet,
And the bright-eyed daisy that grows at its feet.
The lilies white are fair and tall,
But the rose is the fairest flower of all.

div.head: THE BEAUTIFUL GARDEN
div.p: Long ago there was a beautiful garden.
Fair blossoms grew in this garden.
An old apple tree grew there.
In the spring it was beautiful.
In the fall it was covered with apples.
A little daisy grew at its feet.
Her eye was bright and shining.
But all day she looked up and was glad.
A tall lily grew in the garden.
Close beside her grew a rose.
The sweet flowers loved their home.
In the fall the cold wind came to the beautiful garden.
He blew and blew and blew!
“Time to go to sleep, sweet flowers.
The little flowers went to sleep.
The old apple tree saw them.
“Time for me to sleep, too,” she said.
I do not want them now.
They might be cold in the winter.”
The wind blew all the leaves from the old apple tree.
He covered Rose, Daisy, and Lily.
“Now go to sleep, old tree,” he said.
“The beautiful blossoms are all covered with your leaves.
Sleep till spring comes back again.”

div.head: THE GARDEN IN WINTER
div.p: The garden is covered with snow.
Many sweet flowers sleep under the cold white snow.
Daisy is asleep under the apple tree.
They are covered with warm leaves.
The old apple tree is sleeping.
All her buds are sleeping, too.
In the spring they will wake.
Now they are covered with snow.
The snow covers the flowers, too.
For many days they will sleep.
The warm days will come again.
Robin will sing to the flowers.
All the buds and flowers will wake.
They will hear the robin’s song.
They will say, “The warm spring days have come back.”
The garden will be beautiful again.

div.head: ROSE, DAISY, AND LILY
div.p: Rose, Daisy, and Lily grow in a beautiful garden.
These three grow side by side.
Many other flowers are growing all around them.
But none are as beautiful as Rose.
None are as bright-eyed as Daisy.
None are as fair as Lily.
“I was down under the white snow, sound asleep.”
I think I must have been asleep, too.
When I waked, the sun was shining.
It was shining brightly all around.
I felt the warm wind blowing over me.
I saw the snow melting away.
I knew summer would soon be here.
Look! There is little Violet now.
I must stop. My leaves are growing.

div.head: THE SPRING TIME
div.p: Now the days are full of music!
All the birds are back again;
In the tree-tops, in the meadows,
In the woodlands, on the plain.
See them darting through the sunshine!
Hear them singing loud and clear!
How they love the busy spring time—
Sweetest time of all the year!

div.head: TOM AND THE BIRDS
div.p: One morning Tom ran to mother.
“The birds have come back,” said Tom.
“I saw so many in the garden!
They are singing their sweetest songs.
The garden is full of music!
Mother and Tom went into the garden.
Robins were calling from the tree-top.
They were darting in the sunshine.
All were singing their sweetest songs.
They seemed to say, “It is time all nests were made.”
They were so busy and glad.
Robin’s nest was in the apple tree.
The garden was full of music.
“I love to hear the birds sing.”
We must be busy like the birds.

div.head: THE STAR
div.p: A little star lived away up in sky-land.
At night it looked down at the trees.
It looked into the birds’ nest.
It looked long at the sweet flowers.
The little star liked them best of all.
It was always shining on them.
It was always trying to wake them.
One night Mother Moon saw the little star looking down.
“Bright star,” said she, “why are you always shining on the flowers?”
I should like to go and live with them always,” answered the star.
“Do you not love me, little star?”
“Yes, mother dear, I do love you.”
“Do you not love the other stars?”
“Yes, I love you all, but I love the dear flowers best.”
“Then why do you not go to them?” said the sad Mother Moon.
“I will, I will; good-by, good-by,” said the star.
In the morning this little star was gone from the sky.
But a beautiful dandelion was growing in the meadow.

div.head: THE DANDELION’S FRIENDS
div.p: Bright-eyed Daisy grew in the meadow.
All day she looked up at the sky.
It was so bright and blue.
But at night she would close her eye and sleep quietly.
Blue Violet grew in the meadow, too.
She did not always sleep at night.
She looked up into the sky.
She saw a bright star shining there.
She wanted the star to come to her.
One morning Violet and Daisy found a dandelion growing near them.
“Where did you come from, Dandelion?” they asked.
All the long nights through I looked down at you in the meadow.
You looked so sweet and happy here!
I grew to love you dearly.
And I wanted to come down and live with you. So here I am.
Are you glad to see me?
Do you want me to go back to the sky, bright Daisy?
Will you let me stay with you here always, sweet Violet?”

lg.l: Who is it comes with his reindeer,
With a sleigh just full of good things?
Just listen to his sleigh bells!
They are ringing out so clear,
And they tell us as we listen,

div.head: SANTA CLAUS
div.p: Hush! hark! I hear sleigh bells!
Listen and you will hear them.
They are ringing out so clear.
Who can it be? I think I know.
It is just full of good things.
There is something for you and me.
They come rushing, bounding over the ice and snow.
They are coming near, near, nearer!
Hear the bells, loud, loud, louder!
Now do you know who is coming?
Who is coming in his big sleigh?
Who is bounding over ice and snow?
Who brings a sleigh full of good things?

div.head: WHO IS SANTA CLAUS?
div.p: Tom: Christmas will soon be here.
Tom: Why, Baby! Christmas is the time Santa Claus comes.
Tom: He is the friend of all good girls and boys.
Tom: He lives in a cold land far away from here.
Santa Claus comes in a big sleigh.
Baby: Did you see him, Tom?
Tom: No, he comes when all the boys and girls are asleep.
Baby: Why does he come down the chimneys?
Tom: To bring something to all the boys and girls.
Baby: Will he bring something to us?
Tom: He will bring something good.
Baby: What will he bring, Tom?
Tom: You will know in the morning.

div.head: THE NIGHT BEFORE CHRISTMAS
div.p: It was the night before Christmas.
She hung it by the big fire-place.
Then they crept quietly away to bed.
They lay so still, listening, listening.
But not a sound could be heard.
What did they think they would hear?
Soon their tired little eyes were closing.
Outside it was cold, so cold.
Wind was blowing; snow was flying.
Cold clouds hid the blue sky.
Yet over all moon and stars were shining brightly.
At last the moon peeped out.
She peeped through the cold clouds.
She looked far down at the cold world.
Her rays fell upon a beautiful sight.
There was dear old Santa Claus with sleigh and reindeer.
They were flying from house to house.
They were rushing over ice and snow.
In one house he found two stockings.
We know who hung them there.
Santa filled them full as they could hold.
He filled them up to the very top.
How glad Tom and Baby will be!
They have just what they want!”
Back up the chimney Santa went.
Into his big sleigh he jumped.
Then away and away they flew!
So they kept on leaving their good things all the night through.

div.head: THE DOLL AND THE SLED
div.p: Santa had gone up the chimney.
A new sled was by Tom’s stocking.
It was a bright red sled.
“Are you awake, doll?” called the sled.
“Here, in this stocking,” said the doll.
There was a dear little doll peeping out of Baby’s stocking.
“Well, here we are in our new home,” said the doll.
“It is a good home,” said the sled.
“I think we should be happy here.
Santa brought me to the little boy who lives in this house.
I think I will like him.
I know he will like me.
I am so bright and new.”
“He ought to like you,” said the doll.
You are so bright and new.
I am for a dear little girl.
He says she will be kind to me.
He says she will love me.
I know I will love her.
Santa brought her a new hood.
It is such a warm little hood!”
“Who can it be?” asked the doll.
“I think it is mother,” said the sled.
The doll crept back into the stocking.
It lay close to Tom’s stocking.
But not a sound did she hear.
All was quiet till Christmas morning.

div.head: CHRISTMAS MORNING
div.p: “Mother, mother,” they cry, “has Santa Claus been here?
What did he leave for us?
Let’s go look in our stockings quick!”
“Come, Baby, we can feel our way.”
Away they rush to the fire-place.
Mother follows fast with a light.
“Look, mother, look! a sled, a top, a horn, candy.
So many good things!” shouts Tom.
“And here is a warm hood, a big book, and a cup.
My! how many things dear old Santa brought us!”
“Did you know Santa had been here, mother?” asks Tom.
“Did you think he would bring us so many nice things?
I have just what I wanted.”
Mother just smiles sweetly and says:
“Santa Claus has been very kind to you.
I know he thinks you ought to be good.
He will want you to obey mother.”
“That makes me so glad!” says mother.
All three are very happy this beautiful Christmas morning.
The sun is just peeping over the hills.
Tom and Baby are kept busy with their new play-things.

div.head: PLAYING IN THE SNOW
div.p: “Mother, may we go out and play?
May we take our sleds with us?
May we take the ones Santa Claus brought us?
Do say we may go, Mother.”
“You may play in the white snow.
You may take your Christmas sleds.
Come, I will put on your warm coats.”
“Where is my nice hood?” asks Baby.
“I will bring it to you,” answers Tom.
What fun they have in the deep snow!
They are almost covered with it.
How they make the snow fly!
Up the steep hill they run.
They draw their sleds after them.
They ought to look out for the sleighs.
Sometimes the sleds tip over and throw them into the snow.
It is all fun for them.
Now they are making a snow man.
He is made of big balls of snow.
See them throw snow balls at him!
“It is time to come in now.
Come, take off your things by the fire.
Another day you may play out again.
You may play with your sleds.”

lg.l: In the heart of a seed
Too much sun would wither thee;
Butterfly, butterfly, you’re a fairy bright,
Flying high, flying low, in the summer light.

div.head: THE FAIRY BUTTERFLY
div.p: It was a glad summer day.
May was playing in the meadow.
What can it be?” she cried.
“Oh, it is a dear little fairy!
Stop and play, dear fairy,” she cried.
She was too busy to stop.

div.head: THE BUTTERFLY IN THE GARDEN
div.p: One day I saw a beautiful butterfly.
She was flying among the flowers.
But the butterfly made no answer.
But the butterfly just went on playing.
She seemed to be searching for honey.
She flew in and out among the flowers.
And the flowers all love the butterfly.
She flies from flower to flower, now high, now low.
She flies this way and that way.
She likes the sweet bright flowers best of all.
They seem to lift their heads when she comes.
She plays almost all the time.
Would you like to play always?
Would you like to be a butterfly?

div.head: THE LITTLE FAIRY
div.p: A dear little fairy lives in a garden.
The garden is full of beautiful flowers.
The fairy has lived there all summer.
Her thin wings are bright and shining.
All day she flies from flower to flower.
Is she telling them some sweet story?
What do you think she says?
This is what the fairy is saying.
Listen if you want to hear.
The lily is white and tall.
But the rose is the fairest of all.”
Some nights this fairy creeps into the tall white lily.
There she clings through the night.
She does not feel the cold wind.
Other nights she rests in a red rose.
She is buried out of sight.
There she waits for the morning.
She hears the voice of the wind.
The wind blows among the flowers.
It rocks the fairy’s flower cradle.
The stars shine down on her.
She sleeps all the long night.
What a wonderful fairy she is!
What name do we call her?
Sleep, little fairy, sleep and rest,
Of all the flowers, Rose loves you best.

div.head: THE WHITE LILY
div.p: A tall white lily grew in a beautiful garden.
Her home was near the old stone wall.
Her gown was white and shining green.
Lily seemed to know that May loved her.
She lifted her head and smiled at the girl.
Lily could not lift up her head.
Come before all the sweet flowers wither.”
I will be with you soon, dear Lily.”
The bright raindrops fell to the ground.
Faster and faster and faster they came.

div.head: THE CATERPILLAR
div.p: A caterpillar rested on a lily leaf.
He was very big and very green.
“I am so tired,” said the caterpillar. “I can not go away.
“No! No! Go away,” said the lily.
The caterpillar fell from the lily leaf.
In his fall he kept hold of a little twig.
He was tired, so very tired.
He spun a little coat around him.
All winter he slept there soundly.
In the spring the bright sun shone warm.
Its rays fell on the caterpillar’s coat.
And what do you think came out?
A wonderful thing! A beautiful butterfly!
How it flew among the flowers!
It came flying to the lily.
The lily said, “Come, beautiful butterfly, come to my sweet blossoms!
Rest on me—I love you, butterfly!
You are so bright and beautiful!”
But the butterfly answered, “When I was a caterpillar, you did not want me.
You would not let me rest on you then.
You said you did not like caterpillars.
You would not let me stay.
Now I will not stay with you.
I will go to the red rose.
Good-by, lily; you are fair but cold.”

lg.l: What do you do all day?
I just wait here in the tall green grass
Till the children come to play.
What do you do all night?
I wait and wait till the cool dews fall
And my hair grows long and white.
And what do you do when your hair is white
And the children come to play?
They take me up in their dimpled hands
I must search through and through.
To the hive I must carry
All I can this bright day.”

div.head: THE BUSY BEE
div.p: When the weather is fair he is busy all day.
He flies through garden and orchard.
He visits all the sweet flowers.
All little flowers are glad to have him come to them.
The red clover has more honey than many other flowers.
So the bee and the clover are friends.
The bee gathers honey from all the sweet flowers.
He gathers all he can carry.
Over the fields he goes to his hive.
There he stores his honey with care.
He knows the cold winter is coming.
Then he can gather no honey.
There will be no flowers in the fields.
The cold winter winds will blow.
Snow will cover fields and flowers.
But the little bee will be happy.
He will be safe in his snug hive.
There he will keep snug and warm.
Now he can eat his store of honey.
He can eat all he wants.
He will be glad he worked in summer.
He will be glad of his snug warm hive.
He can sleep and rest waiting for another summer.
When it comes he will be busy again.

div.head: WHY THE CLOVER IS SWEET
div.p: A little fairy flew to a daisy.
“Dear Daisy,” she said, “will you give me some honey?”
The fairy flew away to a rose.
“Beautiful Rose,” she said, “will you give me some honey?”
“You may have just a little,” answered the rose.
“I do not care for your honey.”
Away she flew to the clover.
“Little Clover,” she said, “will you give me some honey?”
“Now I will be kind to you.
Hereafter you will have more honey than any other flower.”
And from that day, the clover has been sweet with honey.

div.head: Vocabulary
div.p: Most of the words used in the Aldine Primer are used frequently in this First Reader. The Primer words are not listed in this vocabulary, however; here are given only the words used for the first time in this book.

The number at the left of a word refers to the page on which the story begins in which that word is first used. New words are listed in the text immediately before or after the lesson in which they are used; they are listed after the lesson when they occur in rhymes to be memorized (see Teacher’s Manual), before the lesson in all other cases. Words of series that have already been studied (see Teacher’s Manual) are not usually listed in the text, but are given in this vocabulary.
